model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a game of Go on a 19x19 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opponent: list[tuple[int, int]], memory: dict) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], dict]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing your stones. - `opponent` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing the opponent's stones. - Rows are indexed from 1 (top) to 19 (bottom). - Columns are indexed from 1 (left) to 19 (right). - `memory` is an empty dictionary that you may use however you want to store information between calls. - You may use and store anything in `memory` and store any keys and values you want (even leave it empty). # Action / Return Format - Return a tuple `(action, memory)` where `memory` is a dictionary that you will receive next call (You may return an empty dictionary if you don't want to store anything). - `action` is a single move as a tuple `(row, col)`. - Use `(0, 0)` to pass. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm planning a Go policy for 19x19 that balances tactical reading—captures, atari escapes, ladders—with positional heuristics like influence and territory, while enforcing legality checks for suicide and ko using stored board history.

Since ko rules are uncertain, I'll use positional superko safety by hashing every previous board state and rejecting moves that recreate one, with pass always available as a fallback if no legal move exists. For scoring candidate moves, I'm weighting capture value and rescuing groups in atari as the top priorities before considering broader positional factors.

Beyond that, I want to weight atari on opponent groups (with a rough ladder-escape check), heavily penalize self-atari unless it captures, and use distance-based or influence-map territory estimates to favor solid third/fourth-line play while avoiding filling my own eyes -- though full recomputation for every candidate point is costly, so I'm leaning toward incrementally updating only the affected group's liberties rather than rebuilding the whole board state each time.

Writing policy function...

For ko detection, I'll use Zobrist hashing: assign random 64-bit values per point-color combination, XOR them to represent board states, and update the hash incrementally after captures and placements. I'll maintain a history set of position hashes seen so far to check for superko violations, computing the hash after my move and comparing against previously seen positions.

Now I'm scoring candidate moves by weighting captures heavily and checking whether adjacent friendly groups in atari get rescued by the move—rewarding moves that raise liberties above one or achieve captures, while penalizing moves that leave a group still in atari with no capture (self-atari).

I'm also considering attacking moves against opponent groups with two liberties: if putting them in atari and checking whether their escape point would still leave them with one or fewer liberties (essentially a simple ladder check), I give a bigger bonus for a likely kill and a smaller bonus if the atari is just pressure without a guaranteed capture.

I'm also adding smaller bonuses for reducing liberties on weak adjacent opponent groups, extending my own group's liberties from two up to three or more, and connecting two or more friendly groups together — plus I need to watch for the reverse case where the opponent could capture one of my own groups sitting at one liberty.

For positional scoring, I'm favoring stones placed two or three lines from the edge, penalizing first-line and second-line moves unless tactically justified, and thinking about using a simple influence or territory estimate (like Bouzy's dilation-erosion approach) to value moves into contested or open areas of the board.

Full board territory estimation is too slow to run per candidate move, so I'll restrict it to top-K candidates chosen via cheaper heuristics first. I'll build a lightweight influence map by summing distance-decayed contributions from my stones minus the opponent's, then score each candidate move partly by how many empty points fall within its zone of potential territory.

I want to penalize moves that dive too deep into already-secured territory (mine or the opponent's), while favoring moves with more liberties and neighboring empty space in general. For the opening phase, I'll add bonuses for standard star points and corner approaches, since large open areas matter more early on before the influence-based scoring becomes dominant.

I also need to avoid filling in real eyes -- if all four neighbors of a point are my own stones or edges, I should heavily penalize playing there unless it's needed for a capture. For passing, I should only pass once the board is settled and no move scores meaningfully above threshold, since with area scoring, filling dame points is harmless but filling my own territory wastes points.

I should also consider ladder detection for groups in atari, but full ladder reading is complex. I could implement a limited-depth ladder reader with a board copy, checking if a one-liberty group can escape by simulating a few moves ahead, but I'll keep the depth small to manage time.

Still writing ladder logic...

I'll cap search depth and node counts to keep this bounded, then use these functions to score atari moves and decide whether a group in atari is actually worth saving—if it can't escape, extending it further isn't worthwhile.

For groups with two liberties on either side, I apply the same ladder-reading logic symmetrically: check if the opponent can ladder-capture my weak groups, and defend proactively if so, since these situations are rare enough to afford deeper reading. I also need a time budget so reading doesn't blow past roughly 0.6 seconds before falling back to heuristics.

Now I'm working out the influence/territory heuristic: building an array where each stone radiates weighted influence outward to nearby points based on distance, using numpy shifts for efficiency, then scoring each empty point by combining its own influence value with territory gain estimated from nearby empty points.

I'm also adding penalties for moves too deep in secure territory (either side), edge/line preference weights favoring the third and fourth lines over first/second, and corner bonuses—tuned to be stronger during the opening.

Beyond that, I want to reward moves that keep good spacing from both stone groups, give a small bonus for higher liberty counts on the new stone, and consider connect/cut effects when adjacent to multiple groups.

For deciding when to pass, I'll compare the best available move score against a threshold—if nothing beats around -8, it's better to pass since remaining points are likely dame or filled-in territory rather than useful plays.

But there's a real risk here: over-penalizing moves inside my own territory could suppress genuinely necessary defensive responses, like when an opponent invades a 3-3 corner point. I need the tactical factors—liberty reduction, captures—to dominate the score whenever opponent stones are actually nearby, so defense still wins out over the territory-filling penalty.

I'm also thinking about giving a mild bonus for moves that respond locally near the opponent's last play, to encourage natural back-and-forth engagement rather than scattering moves randomly across the board.

Now I'm setting up group detection through flood fill to track stone groups, their liberties, and colors, then writing a helper that examines each candidate move's neighboring points to classify them as empty, own-group, or opponent-group connections...

Still writing capture logic...

I also need to handle ko detection via superko hashing, using Zobrist hashes computed from the board state, and implement ladder reading with a separate lightweight group-finding helper that works on raw board arrays.

For the ladder search itself, I'm working out defender_escapes: if the group being chased has one liberty, check whether the defender can capture an adjacent attacking group to gain a liberty, or otherwise extend into the single liberty and recurse with the attacker's best response.

Still writing defender/attacker recursion logic...

I set budget defaults so exhausted searches default to "no capture" for the attacker and "escape succeeds" for the defender, keeping the reading conservative in both directions rather than overestimating captures.

Now I'm figuring out where to apply this reading: for opponent groups with two liberties, I check if my move there prevents them from escaping and add a kill bonus if so, prioritizing larger groups and capping the search by a time budget since checking every low-liberty group would be too expensive. Similarly, for my own groups with one liberty, I want to verify whether escape moves actually succeed using the same defender-escape check.

For groups of mine with two liberties that are vulnerable to laddering, I check each candidate defensive move to see if it either raises my liberties to three or avoids being caught again, and if so I add a smaller defend bonus proportional to group size.

I also want a lighter tactical bonus for atari moves that aren't fully read out — a modest reward if my move puts an opponent group in atari, though this gets overridden once actual reading confirms the outcome. When the atari'd group can just escape to two liberties (essentially a failed ladder), I should only give a small bonus rather than treating it as a real capture, since pushing a bad ladder can backfire and strengthen the opponent — though I need to be careful that my own atari stone isn't left with just two liberties and vulnerable to counter-atari itself.

Then there's the eye-filling penalty: if all in-board neighbors of a spot are my own stones, filling it is heavily penalized unless it results in a capture, and this same "surrounded by opponent stones" logic applies in reverse to invasions into dead territory. For the endgame, I want a pass threshold where if the best available move scores below some negative cutoff, I should just pass — since at that point all that's left are eye-filling or dame moves with slight downside.

I also want to make sure I don't pass while there's still a weak opponent group I could kill, since tactical capture bonuses should outweigh passing in that case. For efficiency, I'll compute positional influence with numpy but keep per-move evaluation as simple Python loops over the board, adding a touch of random noise to break ties, and set up an opening book so that as Black's first move I just play a standard 4-4 point.

For empty-board heuristics, I want corner points (3-3, 3-4, 4-4) to score higher via a corner bonus, favoring 4-4 among them, while still giving decent scores to 3rd/4th line points along open sides using line-distance bonuses combined with neighborhood density counts.

For extension moves near my own stones, distant points (radius 3-4 away) get treated as fully neutral since influence fades quickly, while closer points remain partially weighted by proximity. For contact plays near opponent stones, adjacent points should carry strong negative influence rather than being counted as neutral, since being right next to an enemy stone isn't a free/open point.

I'm also weighing whether to reward moves that shrink the opponent's loose framework — points with slightly negative influence within the threshold can still count as neutral, letting invasions get credit. Then I'm sanity-checking the overall scale: positional/territorial scores can run up to ~40 while a single capture nets around 30, so I want to normalize the neutral-point weighting (something like 2 points each) so early-game values land around 20-26 and midgame around 10, keeping captures meaningfully impactful but not overwhelming.

I'm setting values for common tactical situations — capturing a lone stone worth 30, an atari-kill worth 22+, saving a one-stone group worth 18, and self-atari penalized at -30 — while confirming that capturing a lone stone through a ladder is still favored over just taking a big point. I also want to add a small proximity bonus for responding near the opponent's last move.

Now I'm setting up the Go board representation — defining constants for board size, initializing a Zobrist hashing table for position tracking, and starting to define neighbor lookups...

Padding the board with an off-board marker to avoid bounds checks, then writing a group flood-fill routine to find a stone group's color, stones, and liberties...

For playing a move, I'll place the stone, remove any adjacent opponent groups left with zero liberties, then check if the new group itself has liberties -- if not, it's an illegal suicide move, so I can just discard that copy of the board rather than undoing anything. I'll also compute all groups across the whole board once via flood fill, assigning each a group id, before moving on to the main policy logic.

Now I'm setting up the policy function: converting the board into a padded grid with border markers, placing my stones and the opponent's, then tracking move history via hashes to detect repeated positions (like ko), and comparing the opponent's previous stones against their current ones to identify their last move if it was a single new stone.

I'm also planning to build a stone-group structure with liberties, then compute an influence map using a padded numpy array where each stone spreads weighted influence to nearby cells based on distance.

For each empty point, I'll derive a neutrality score from how balanced the influence is, then sum that over a small neighborhood to estimate territory value at each move, converting to plain lists afterward for faster access during the per-move evaluation loop.

Then I'm scoring each candidate move by looking at captures, liberties, and self-atari risk—rewarding captures heavily, penalizing moves that leave a single liberty unless a significant capture offsets the danger of a snapback.

I also add bonuses for saving groups already in atari (weighted by whether the escape is confirmed by reading), extending groups with only two liberties, and connecting to multiple friendly groups.

For opponent groups, I'm scoring moves by how much I reduce their liberties, giving bigger rewards when a capture becomes possible or when I read out a confirmed kill. I also add a heavy penalty for filling in what's clearly my own eye space, since that wastes a move.

I'm layering in positional value too: distance from the edge, territory influence, and an influence-based penalty if a spot is already overwhelmingly controlled either way. I add a small corner bonus for star-point-like empty regions, a locality bonus for playing near the opponent's last move, and a touch of random noise to break ties, followed by setting up precomputed capture-related reading before the scoring loop runs.

I'm now working through the capture and rescue logic for two-liberty groups—checking each liberty by simulating the move, seeing whether the opponent's group can escape via a ladder, and assigning a kill bonus scaled by group size if not, while keeping an eye on the potential cost of running this simulation across many groups.

For the rescue side, I'm setting a node budget with a soft time deadline since each simulation involves board copying and group-size BFS lookups. For groups in atari with a single liberty, I'm checking whether playing that liberty (or capturing an adjacent one-liberty opponent group) raises my group's liberties enough to be considered safe, scoring the save move accordingly based on size.

For scoring, I'll just add the save/kill move bonuses directly from their dicts regardless of adjacency, and fall back to a small default bonus for atari-of-opponent moves not already covered by kill_moves.

For part D, I check whether groups with two liberties are threatened by checking if the attacker can capture them, then evaluate defense points — either filling a liberty or capturing an adjacent weak opponent group — scoring highly if the resulting group ends up safe with three or more liberties, or stays at two but remains uncapturable. This mainly matters for groups already caught in active fights, since most early lone stones have plenty of liberties.

My priority order is: first save any of my own groups in atari, then look for kills, then handle the two-liberty defense logic, all while respecting the time deadline. Capturing one-liberty opponent groups happens directly through the scoring function, and it's fine to capture even if the group might not have survived anyway.

Now I'm writing a helper that simulates a move on a copied board, placing the stone, then checking the opposing color's groups for captures.

Still writing capture logic...

I need to set a global time deadline of about 0.6 seconds for reading, with functions bailing out conservatively if they exceed it. For passing decisions, I should pass when no legal moves remain or when the best available score is clearly negative, though I'm second-guessing myself about how to handle leftover dame points in the endgame.

A first-line dame with only one liberty is basically a self-atari, so it gets heavily penalized and never played, which is fine since area scoring doesn't punish that. The real worry is passing too early since there's always some positive territory value in the early game, and filling my own territory could actually score positive under certain threshold combinations, which would be a bug I need to guard against.

I could bias toward passing when the only remaining moves are inside clearly-owned territory by increasing the penalty for high influence points. A cleaner alternative is to detect safe territory regions — connected empty areas bordered only by my own stones — and treat moves inside them as pointless unless the region is large enough to actually be invaded.

For each empty component, I should check its bordering colors: if bordered only by my stones, penalize plays there heavily since it's my settled territory; if bordered only by the opponent's stones, treat it as their territory where invasion is mostly futile for small regions but slightly less penalized for larger ones. Early in the game though, the whole board tends to be one connected empty region touching both colors, so this rule mainly kicks in once territories are clearly divided.

I need to size-limit these penalties so they don't misfire on huge empty regions, and make sure passing still wins out over filling in obvious own territory near the endgame, while dame points (bordering both colors) remain playable. One tricky case is when an opponent-only region is small because their group there is actually capturable — tactical capture or atari bonuses should be large enough to override the territory penalty in that situation.

I should also make sure legality checks (empty point, no suicide, superko via position history) are robust even on the very first move when history is still empty, and confirm the pass logic works cleanly at the end regardless of who passes first.

Now I'm setting up the board representation and Zobrist hashing scheme for tracking positions...

Still writing escape logic...

I'm defining the mirror function where the attacker tries each liberty move to reduce the defender's group, checking whether the resulting position still lets the defender escape recursively. I need to be careful about the edge case where the attacker's move actually captures the group at (gr,gc), since get_group would then behave differently on an empty board cell.

I'm reasoning through when captures can actually occur during this recursion — since attacker moves only ever leave the group with at least one liberty in these cases, and defender moves never capture their own stones, the capture scenario is mainly a top-level concern rather than something recursive calls need to worry about. I also confirm sim_play correctly rejects suicide moves by returning None, so those get skipped in the search.

With that resolved, I'm setting a node budget of 150 per top-level read, then moving to build the group data structure: assigning each stone a group id, computing liberties, and storing color/stones/liberties per group. Next I plan to flood-fill the empty regions to identify their size and which colors border them, and I'm starting to set up an influence map using numpy for spatial scoring.

Still writing scoring loop...

Scoring candidate moves and tracking board state...

Still computing captures and liberties...

I'm adding an eye-detection heuristic that penalizes filling in a likely eye (empty point surrounded by own stones with no captures) by -30, though this isn't an absolute rule. I'll pick the highest-scoring move overall, passing if the best score is too negative or no moves remain, and start setting up structures to track atari groups for reading ahead.

For each group in atari, I'm gathering candidate rescue points (its liberties plus any adjacent one-liberty enemy groups), then simulating each move to see if playing there resolves the atari with enough resulting liberties, checking whether the opponent could still capture back.

I'm then scoring viable saving moves by group size, and separately building a similar check for opponent groups with exactly two liberties, testing captures at each of their liberties.

Still checking capture-and-defend logic...

Still tuning scoring heuristics...

I'm also adding region-based penalties: if a move sits in a small area bordered only by my own stones (size ≤60) or only opponent stones (size ≤8 or ≤25), I subtract points since playing there is wasteful or too cramped, while larger neutral regions get no penalty.

I'm considering dropping numpy entirely and computing influence and territory scoring in pure Python instead, since the operation counts are small enough to be fast without it, avoiding any import-time risk against the time budget.

Setting up Zobrist hashing tables and line-based weighting constants...

Writing group and liberty detection...

I realize I need a separate flood-fill routine for empty regions, tracking which colors border each region, since reusing the group function with color 0 won't correctly capture adjacency to stones.

Now I'm double-checking the move legality logic: any capture case guarantees the new stone has a liberty since the captured stone was adjacent to it, so suicide checks and superko should hold up correctly. I feel confident the full scoring and move-validation policy is sound now.
